uncited: This method distributes the rendering workload of a single volume dataset across multiple GPUs on a single node by interleaving data partitions and switching rendering contexts per frame.
It solves the problem of memory capacity limits and throughput bottlenecks in single-GPU rendering by leveraging multiple graphics cards to process disjoint subsets of the volume data simultaneously.

It differs from general multi-GPU setups by enforcing a strict sequential context switching model combined with pixel-wise result combination, rather than independent frame rendering or complex inter-GPU communication protocols.
The volume data is organized as a sorted array of voxels with associated detail coefficients for each pyramid level.
- **Voxel Data**: Each voxel entry includes position and intensity attributes.
**Data Distribution**: Distribute the interleaved voxel data and histogram to the respective GPU memory.
Render the volume subset assigned to the first GPU.
Read the resulting image back to system memory using `glReadPixels`.
Render the volume subset assigned to the second GPU, which now composites over the first GPU's result.
g. (Repeat for additional GPUs if applicable, chaining the read/write operations).
**Result Combination**: The final image is obtained from the last GPU in the chain.
- **No Direct Inter-GPU Transfer**: There is no extension for direct data shuffling between cards.
Intermediate results must pass through the CPU.
- **Multi-threading Inefficiency**: Attempting to run rendering loops for multiple contexts in separate threads yields no performance gain.
- **Time Complexity**: The rendering time is dominated by the GPU computation, which is roughly halved per additional GPU (linear speedup in ideal conditions).
- **Memory Complexity**: Memory usage is distributed.
- **Strengths**: Simple implementation using standard OpenGL extensions; supports volumes exceeding single-GPU memory; effective for MIP rendering.
- **When to use**: When rendering very large volumes on a single node with multiple NVIDIA GPUs and when the bottleneck is VRAM or single-GPU throughput, and inter-GPU latency is tolerable.
- **When not to use**: When low latency is critical, or when using hardware that supports direct peer-to-peer GPU communication (e.g., NVLink) which would bypass the CPU bottleneck.
This method originates from research on multiresolution MIP rendering of large volumetric data accelerated on graphics hardware.
It was developed to support datasets that exceed the memory capacity of a single graphics card.
